posts.title: How its moveing
posts.excerpt: Polling trends in each state and primary results
posts.body:
Since the start of August there have been 13 primaries held as of writing. The dominating story of the primaries has continued to be the establishment Democrats fighting off the progressive insurgents. There have been wins and losses for both sides. The Michigan primary was a notable win for progressives when Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated Haley Stevens after being outspent by millions. The establishment did have their fair share of wins, notably in Missouri and Wisconsin with Cori Bush and Francisco Hong both losing. On the Republican side, primaries have not been nearly as dramatic, though famous pillow salesman Mike Lindell, a Trump-endorsed candidate, lost his primary for Minnesota governor and stated that there was election fraud in the state (which is BS).

There hasn't been too many changes in already established races though there has been some good polling for both Peltola in Alaska and Talarico. Right now unless there are changes in the state of the race the trends are starting to establish themselves. Always keep in mind that anything can happen though and what looks like a certainty now could change entirely by election day.

posts.title: Polling discrepancies
posts.excerpt: It's all a fugazi, it's fairy dust
posts.body:
When looking at polls that try to predict an election result, like the generic ballot or statewide races, it can be hard to get a clear picture of the information available. One thing I’ve noticed is that all adults, registered voters, and the people who actually vote on Election Day can be very different groups. For example, a large majority of the population might like a candidate, but when it comes time to vote, many of them may not show up. This is called voting propensity and is usually used to describe how likely certain groups are to vote.

Right now, this effect tends to benefit Democrats, although it has not always been that way. Polling companies try to account for it through sampling and other adjustments, but it is still hard to know exactly who will vote on Election Day. As fewer people respond to polls, it becomes even harder to track. Polling companies will keep making adjustments, and my site tries to do the same, but there is no way to perfectly predict what the electorate will look like. In the end, a lot of it is still a crapshoot, and no one really knows what will happen until the votes are counted.

posts.title: New Features
posts.body:
I added the ability to create maps and simulate elections. The map-making tool is based on other tools I have used, combining the parts I liked while remaining functional. It is not anything revolutionary, but it allows both me and other users to create maps and save them directly to the site.

The second feature I added is an election simulator. It includes several customizable options and allows users to test the predictions made on the site in real time.

posts.title: Maine senate changes and Gallup Poll
posts.excerpt: Graham Platner leaves Maine senate race And Gallup releases party Id poll
posts.body:
First , Graham Platner has dropped out of the Maine Senate race after allegations of rape came out. This kinda just adds to all the controversies this guy already had, and there was too much pressure for him not to drop out. Platner has been plagued by controversy, and this one was really just the nail in the coffin. The Maine Senate race is going to stay where it was because, without a candidate, it basically just goes back to the baseline. There is also no polling data for whoever the new candidate will be.

In other news, Gallup released its party ID poll, which looks to give Democrats their biggest advantage since 2009. The party ID poll is one of the most accurate things, at least historically, when predicting the makeup of the electorate and the national popular vote. There is a lot of discrepancy between national and state polls right now, and the party ID poll does not really help clear the waters there.

posts.title: Release and happy 4th
posts.body:
Happy Fourth of July and happy 250th!

This is the official release of my site. It has been a summer project for me, and I hope it can help provide candidate and polling information for the next election in an easy-to-understand way. The ability to change is one of the most important parts of our country, and in my opinion, it is what has allowed this country to thrive. Elections have always been important to me because they are a way for people to create change. That interest and passion for elections and change is what pushed me to create this site, so hopefully it can help others get interested and participate in that change too.
Once again, happy Fourth, and be safe today.

posts.title: Explaining data
posts.body: Some of my predictions might seem to favor Democrats more than others out there. This is primarily because I account for voting propensity, or the likelihood that individual groups will actually vote in the election and which party they are favoring. Looking at that can give a better picture of the results, especially because national and statewide polls can be inaccurate since it is hard to predict who will actually vote. This same model was used to predict the results in 2024 and was accurate, so hopefully it holds again.
